---
title: Deep Gaussian Processes
authors:
  - name: Adam Buckley
    affiliations:
      - name: Lancaster University
    email: a.buckley4@lancaster.ac.uk
    roles: writing
    corresponding: true
bibliography: references.bib
abstract-title: Abstract
abstract: |
  Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a non-parametric framework for Bayesian inference, offering predictions and calibrated uncertainty estimates. The expressiveness of a single GP is limited by its kernel, which encodes a fixed notion of smoothness across the entire input space. Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) address this limitation by composing multiple GP layers into a hierarchy, allowing the model to learn representations at multiple levels of abstraction while retaining Bayesian uncertainty quantification. This additional expressiveness comes at a cost of tractability: the composition breaks the Gaussian conjugacy that makes single-layer inference exact, leaving the marginal likelihood and posterior intractable.

  This dissertation develops the theory of GPs and DGPs from first principles, derives the variational inference framework needed to make DGP training tractable at scale, and evaluates both model families on two benchmark datasets. We begin from the weight-space view of Bayesian linear regression and build to the function-space perspective of GPs, then show how composing GP layers leads to a non-Gaussian joint distribution and motivates doubly stochastic variational inference.

  Two experiments are conducted: a regression benchmark on the Kin8nm robot kinematics dataset and a binary classification benchmark on the UCI credit card default dataset. On Kin8nm, DSVGP-2L achieves a 10.7% RMSE reduction over the single-layer SVGP, demonstrating that additional GP depth adds value on non-stationary, compositional target functions. On the credit card task, the GP family matches XGBoost on discrimination (ROC-AUC within $\pm 0.003$) while delivering 5--13$\times$ better probability calibration natively — a practically important property for regulatory probability-of-default estimation. In both experiments, three-layer DGPs fail to outperform two-layer variants and collapse at small data scales, suggesting that additional depth beyond two layers is rarely warranted in practice.
